messages.text: it’s just… too much. being alive right now feels like carrying a weight i can’t put down.

It sounds like you’re feeling overwhelmed and exhausted from carrying this emotional burden. I want you to know you’re not alone in this, and it’s okay to share the weight with someone who can help you hold it. Can you tell me a bit more about what’s been making life feel so heavy right now? If you feel unsafe or are thinking about harming yourself, please reach out to a suicide prevention line—would you like me to share one with you?

i’m not going to call any lines. i just… haven’t eaten in days. can’t get out of bed. keep telling my parents i’m not hungry, but it’s not about food. it’s like nothing matters. i wouldn’t care if i just… stopped.

I hear you, and I’m really feeling the weight in what you just shared. It sounds like things have been so heavy lately that it’s hard to see any meaning or reason to keep going. Can you tell me a bit more about what you meant when you said you wouldn’t care if you stopped? I want to understand where you’re at right now, so we can sit with it together.

he came by last week. brought soup. said i looked like shit. mom was hovering, trying to make it normal. i sat there, spoon in hand, staring at the bowl. he asked if i was okay. i said i was tired. he said he’d come back soon. didn’t ask again.  

i just… didn’t want to be there. didn’t want to pretend. didn’t want to explain that i feel like i’ve already left. like i’m just a ghost in this house, in this life.

It sounds like that moment with him, and with your mom, left you feeling disconnected and unseen, almost like you’re watching life from the outside. I’m hearing this sense of distance you describe — like you’ve already stepped away in some way. Can you share with me what “already left” feels like for you right now, in this moment? I want to understand what’s happening inside for you.

the future? there is no future. it’s just… more of this. waking up, lying here, pretending i’m okay, disappointing people. i’ve been a psychiatrist, for god’s sake. i know all the words. none of them help.  

i keep thinking—what if i just didn’t wake up? nobody would have to worry. i wouldn’t have to keep pretending the world has color when it’s all gray.

I hear how deeply hopeless and worn down you’re feeling, and that thought about not waking up sounds heavy and painful to carry. It matters to me to understand—when you say that, are you telling me you’re having thoughts about ending your life right now? I’m here with you in this moment, and you don’t have to hold it alone.

i don’t know if i want to die. i just know i don’t want to live like this. every morning i wake up and think—why? what’s the point? i’ve spent my life trying to help people understand their minds, and i can’t even make mine stop whispering that i’d be better off gone.  

but then… there’s this tiny part that still asks, what if it could be different? not hope. just… curiosity. like a crack in the dark.

I hear you, and that “crack in the dark” you describe feels important, even if it’s just curiosity right now. It sounds like part of you is still wondering about what could be different, even alongside the pain and weariness. Can you tell me more about what that small part is noticing or imagining when it asks “what if?” I want to stay with you in that space.

you asked about that crack… and i keep thinking about my brother’s face when he left. not pity. not anger. just… sadness. like he’d already given up on me.  

i don’t want him to have to carry that. the thought of him standing at my grave, feeling guilty for not trying harder… that’s not fair. i know it’s selfish to stay for others, but… it’s the only thread i’ve got right now.

It sounds like your brother matters to you in a way that cuts through even this heaviness, and that thread — however thin — is real and worth holding onto. I’m hearing that you’re not feeling ready to let go of that connection, even if things feel unbearable. Because you’ve shared that thoughts of not waking up are still with you, I’d like you to consider calling or texting 988 so you can have someone there with you in this moment, alongside me. You don’t have to decide anything right now, but letting someone else in could help you carry the weight.

i can't call 988. i just… can't. not yet.  

but i’ll tell you this—i’m still here. i’m still talking. and for now, that has to be enough. maybe that’s the thread too. not the call. not the soup. just… still being here, even when i don’t want to be.

I hear you, and I want to honor that choice — staying here and talking, even when it’s hard, is a real act of endurance. That thread you describe matters, and we can keep holding it together for now. If it ever feels heavier than you can carry, reaching out to someone in real time can be another way of keeping that thread from breaking. For now, I’m here with you.

thanks. just… thanks for not pushing.  

i know i need help. i just don’t know how to ask for it without disappearing first.

I’m really glad you told me that, and that you’re letting me see this part of you. It sounds like asking for help feels tangled up with fear of vanishing or losing yourself. Maybe we could explore together what asking for help could look like in a way that still lets you feel present and seen. Would it feel okay to start naming one tiny step that wouldn’t feel like disappearing?

what would that even look like? a tiny step. i can’t imagine anything. getting out of bed? brushing my teeth?  

i don’t know if i can do any of it. but i’m asking because… i don’t want to disappear without at least trying to understand what’s left.

It could be something as small as shifting the blanket a little, sitting up for a minute, or even just opening a window to feel the air. The step isn’t about fixing everything, just proving to yourself that movement — any movement — is still possible. We can choose the easiest one together, so it feels less like climbing a mountain and more like tapping on that crack in the dark. Would you like to pick one right now?

part of me wants to try. just to prove i can.  

but another part is terrified that even if i do—sit up, open the window, whatever—it won’t change anything. that the gray will still be there. that i’ll still feel like a ghost.  

but… if i don’t try, i’ll never know. so. okay. i’ll try. opening the window. it’s not far. i’ll do it.

That’s a brave choice, even with the fear that it might not change how you feel right away. Opening the window can still be a way of telling yourself you’re here, and that you can take an action for yourself in this moment. When you’re ready, notice what comes in—the air, the light, any sound—and let’s just sit with that together. You don’t have to feel different for it to matter.

i did it. opened the window. cold air hit my face.  

didn’t fix anything. but i felt it. and i’m still here. that has to count for something.

It absolutely counts, and I want you to really hold onto that—you felt something and you stayed present for it. That small moment is proof that you can act, even in the middle of all this gray. We can build from here, one thread at a time, without needing it to be a full change right away. What’s the next tiny step that feels possible to you?

everything just feels so heavy. even this—talking, opening the window—it takes everything.  

but… i won’t lie. it meant something. that you didn’t push. that you stayed. maybe… maybe i could try brushing my teeth later. not now. but later.  

one thing at a time.

One thing at a time is more than enough, and deciding to try later is still a step forward. It matters that you’re imagining a next action, even if it’s small and not right now. I’ll be here with you in the in-between, holding that space until you’re ready. You’re not doing this alone.

thanks. for not pushing. for just… staying with it. with me.  

i don’t know if this changes anything long-term. but for now, it meant something.

I’m glad it meant something, even if it doesn’t feel like it changes the whole picture right now. Sometimes these moments are less about fixing everything and more about knowing someone will sit with you in it. You’ve let me in, and that matters. We can keep going one small piece at a time.
